title: The Brutal History of The First Warplanes
dek: At the start of World War I, aircraft were dismissed as a joke by the officer class; within four years, the sky became a meat grinder of reconnaissance, bombing, and dogfighting, with new pilots in 1917 averaging about two weeks of life.
why: Joshua Levine uses diaries and archives to make the evolution of air combat from child's play to industrial meat grinder extremely concrete; his analysis in the middle and later sections of why aces broke their own rules and died is especially rare.
who: Defense and hard-tech investors, founders studying the pace of technology iteration, and team leaders trying to understand why top talent self-destructs.
skip: Channel promotions and ad breaks can be skipped; the main content has almost no filler.

points.h: Britain's first plane came from a Wild West showman
points.body: At the start of the war, senior officers still saw cavalry as the main reconnaissance force and were both snobbish and impatient with aircraft: airships were treated as a gentleman's mode of transport, while heavier-than-air machines were dirty, noisy, and needed mechanics, so they were dismissed as 'not for our kind of people.' Britain's first plane came from an American, Samuel Cody—he originally came to Britain with a Wild West show, posing as Buffalo Bill's cousin and performing tricks like shooting eggs off his wife's head, before turning to flight. His large aircraft was nicknamed the 'flying birdcage' because it was big enough to hold a canary. Cody later died in a flying accident, which was the norm in early aviation.

points.h: The commander-in-chief only cared if it was cold up there, not about intelligence
points.body: The Royal Flying Corps' initial task was to reconnoiter German movements over France, but the start was almost farcical: two pilots both got lost; one landed and nearly was captured, then was recognized and instead taken to dinner by the mayor; the other was so disoriented that he flew over a large city before realizing it was Brussels. Yet they soon began reporting genuinely useful intelligence. One pilot sketched what he saw on his knee board and reported back to Sir John French, but French was not interested in the intelligence—he only asked if it was cold up there and how far one could see. French's skepticism later proved completely wrong, and aircraft were gradually taken seriously.

points.h: Aircraft changed war with eyes, not machine guns
points.body: The most critical air achievement of WWI was not shooting down but seeing. On September 13, observer Atkinson's report twice noted 'trenches are being dug in the fields.' Joshua says this was the beginning of everything—from then on, the Western Front entered trench warfare, and reconnaissance aircraft went from dispensable novelties to truly essential eyes and ears. Later that same day, Sir John French formally issued a commendation to the flying corps. In other words, aircraft changed war not because of machine guns but because they were the only eyes that could see the whole battlefield.

points.h: Bombing was not designed by generals; pilots figured it out
points.body: Bombing and air combat were not designed by generals but tried out by pilots themselves. Initially they dropped steel darts, then hand grenades, and only later strapped on bombs. One pilot cut a hole in the bottom of his fuselage and lined it with tin to form a chute, intending to drop bombs that way, but the airflow narrowed the tin and jammed the bomb, leaving the detonator exposed beneath the belly. He passed a note to Louis Strange that read, 'We are going to die.' The two chose to land and wait for the explosion, but the tall corn in the field pulled the detonator off, and they escaped unharmed. Louis Strange later died peacefully in bed at an old age—that was the daily reality of early flight.

points.h: One mechanical device made every Allied plane obsolete overnight
points.body: To fire a machine gun through the propeller, the Dutchman Fokker first offered the solution to the Allies; they declined, so he turned to building aircraft for Germany. His mechanical device allowed bullets to fire only in the gaps between propeller blades, suddenly letting German pilots aim head-on, and instantly making all existing Allied aircraft obsolete—'going up meant going to die.' This moment is equivalent to today's drones on the Ukrainian front becoming obsolete within weeks of arrival—WWI air combat itself was an arms race measured in months, even weeks.

points.h: Average life of two weeks, yet with orderlies and a roller-skating rink
points.body: Fighter pilots lived a life of extremes. During the 1917 Battle of Arras, the average time from a new pilot's arrival at the front to death was only about two weeks; many were sent into battle with severely inadequate training, and conditions like 'flying sickness'—a mental breakdown treated with more leniency—appeared. Yet at the same time, they were housed behind the front lines, with orderlies, could go into town for drinks, had favorite restaurants, and one squadron commander even poured concrete himself to build a roller-skating rink. Comfort and fear coexisted—that was the daily life of a fighter pilot.

points.h: Too-famous aces may have chosen the time of their death
points.body: Richthofen and McCudden both wrote down their own air combat rules, such as 'after shooting down an enemy, do not follow him down over his own lines,' because low altitude made you a target for ground rifles and machine guns. Yet these two most elite, most symbolic pilots ultimately died precisely by violating their own rules. Joshua does not accept the explanation that 'they thought they were above the rules' and offers a possibility: because they were so famous, they were kept continuously at the front, and subconsciously knowing they would die sooner or later, they chose to end it at a time and place they could control, rather than wait for the enemy to choose.
